topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Knowing our numbers
topic.scope: place value, Indian and international systems, comparing and ordering large numbers, estimation and rounding, Roman numerals

misconceptions.statement: The value of a digit is the same regardless of its position.
misconceptions.why: Students often focus on the face value of the digit rather than its positional weight.
misconceptions.fix: The value of a digit is determined by its place (ones, tens, hundreds, etc.) in the number.

probe.question: What is the value of 5 in 502?

misconceptions.root_belief: a digit is a static object

misconceptions.statement: Commas are placed after every two digits regardless of the system.
misconceptions.why: Overgeneralization of the Indian system pattern.
misconceptions.fix: The Indian system uses commas after 3 digits then every 2, while the International system uses commas every 3 digits.
misconceptions.root_belief: one rule works for all contexts

misconceptions.statement: A number with more digits is always larger.
misconceptions.why: This is true for whole numbers, but students fail to consider decimals or leading zeros.
misconceptions.fix: While true for whole numbers, comparing numbers requires looking at the highest place value first.

misconceptions.why: Students often memorize a partial rule without understanding the midpoint convention.
misconceptions.fix: By convention, 5 is rounded up to the next higher ten or hundred.

misconceptions.statement: Roman numerals can be repeated as many times as needed to make a number.
misconceptions.why: Students treat Roman symbols like tally marks.
misconceptions.fix: Symbols like I, X, C can be repeated at most three times.

misconceptions.statement: In the Indian system, the place after thousands is called ten thousands and then millions.
misconceptions.why: Student mixes Indian and international names for higher places because both are taught together.
misconceptions.fix: In the Indian system the places go Ones, Tens, Hundreds, Thousands, Ten Thousands, Lakhs, Ten Lakhs, Crores. 'Million' belongs to the international system.

probe.question: Write 10,00,000 in words using the Indian system.

misconceptions.root_belief: Names of places are the same in both systems

misconceptions.statement: One million is equal to 1,00,000 because it has five zeros like a lakh.
misconceptions.why: Student confuses the sizes of lakh and million and counts zeros loosely.
misconceptions.fix: 1 million = 10 lakh = 10,00,000 (seven digits, six zeros). 1 lakh = 1,00,000 has five zeros.

probe.question: How many lakhs make one million?

misconceptions.root_belief: Lakh and million are the same size

misconceptions.statement: If two numbers have the same number of digits, the one with the bigger last digit is greater.
misconceptions.why: Student compares from the right (ones place) instead of the leftmost digit.
misconceptions.fix: Compare digits from the leftmost place; the first place where they differ decides which number is greater.
misconceptions.root_belief: Comparison starts from the ones digit
misconceptions.source_hint: misconception research on whole number comparison

misconceptions.statement: To round to the nearest hundred, you look at the ones digit.
misconceptions.why: Student applies the rounding procedure without tying the deciding digit to the place being rounded.
misconceptions.fix: To round to the nearest hundred, look at the tens digit. 5 or more rounds up, less than 5 rounds down.

probe.question: Round 3,463 to the nearest hundred.
probe.wrong_answer: 3,500 (because 3 in the ones place is less than 5, so... 3,460)

misconceptions.root_belief: Always check the last digit when rounding

misconceptions.statement: When rounding, every digit after the rounding place becomes a 9 if rounding down.
misconceptions.why: Student mixes rounding down with 'one less than' idea, or leaves the digits unchanged instead of replacing with zeros.
misconceptions.fix: After rounding, all digits to the right of the rounded place become zeros, e.g. 3,463 rounds to 3,500.
misconceptions.root_belief: Rounded digits keep or change arbitrarily

misconceptions.statement: A smaller Roman symbol written before a bigger one is added, so IX means 11.
misconceptions.why: Student reads left to right and adds everything, ignoring the subtractive rule.
misconceptions.fix: A smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted: IX = 10 − 1 = 9. Placed after, it is added: XI = 11.

probe.question: Write the value of IV in our number system.

misconceptions.root_belief: Roman symbols are always added left to right
misconceptions.source_hint: mathematics education research on Roman numerals

misconceptions.statement: Any smaller Roman symbol can be subtracted from any larger one, so VX is 5 and IC is 99.
misconceptions.why: Student overgeneralises the subtraction rule without knowing which symbols can be subtracted from which.
misconceptions.fix: Only I, X and C can be subtracted, and only from the next two larger symbols (I from V and X; X from L and C; C from D and M). V, L and D are never subtracted. So 5 is V, and 99 is XCIX.
misconceptions.root_belief: Subtraction rule works for any pair of symbols
